extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English literature; poets and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Critical lecture-style guidance on what makes poetry (and poets) good or defective: criteria include authenticity, style, unity, imagination, construction, and suitability of subject and temperament. Practical examples and anti-patterns are given through assessments of contemporary poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for truth and nature, not for reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the restless candidate for praise takes no pleasure, no sincere and heartfelt delight in his works, but as they are admired and applauded by others, what should others see in them to admire or applaud?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentic poetic production must begin from an inward love of truth and nature. Examples: Raphael, Titian, Shakespeare are invoked as artists thinking of their subject rather than of themselves; the anti-pattern is working primarily to lay violent hands on reputation or to mortgage one's work for a newspaper puff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patience and trust in posterity over seeking instant applause
rubrics_metrics.description: Those minds, then, which are the most entitled to expect it, can best put up with the postponement of their claims to lasting fame. No applause, however loud and violent, can anticipate or over-rule the judgment of posterity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good poets can afford to wait; works with 'seeds of immortality' will survive. Critics and poets alike should husband enthusiasm and not expend all praise on untried contemporary reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid personal acquaintance bias when judging contemporaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal intercourse with living authors, while it takes away all real relish or freedom of opinion with regard to their contemporaries, greatly lessens the likelihood of forming an impartial critical judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: familiarity may make critics either unduly deferential or unduly prejudiced. Poets rarely praise one another in hyperbole; therefore critics should guard against personal prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic characters should reflect natural, varied passions (avoid moral puppetry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Miss Baillie ... with her the passions are, like the French republic, one and indivisible: they are not so in nature, or in Shakespeare. She treats her grown men and women as little girls treat their dolls — makes moral puppets of them, pulls the wires, and they talk virtue and act vice, according to their cue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In drama, characters must exhibit genuine complexity and natural mixture of passions rather than static, didactic types constructed to illustrate a single moral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and truth of expression over ornamented, far-fetched diction
rubrics_metrics.description: He wraps up obvious thoughts in a glittering cover of fine words; is full of enigmas with no meaning to them; is studiously inverted, and scrupulously far-fetched: and his verses are poetry, chiefly because no particle, line, or syllable of them reads like prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the Delia Cruscan style: tortuous, teazing, or ambiguous phrasing that hides thought. Truth of nature and intelligibility are preferred to finery that prevents seeing the thought for the ambiguity of the language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression must serve substance, not substitute for it
rubrics_metrics.description: A painful attention is paid to the expression in proportion as there is little to express, and the decomposition of prose is substituted for the composition of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't over-elaborate expression when the underlying idea is weak; the composition of poetry requires substantial ideas, not merely polished surfaces or verbal epigrams that mask poverty of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hypercriticism and paralysing self-censure
rubrics_metrics.description: He plays the hypercritic on himself, and starves his genius to death from a needless apprehension of a plethora. No writer who thinks habitually of the critics, either to tremble at their censures or set them at defiance, can write well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive fear of criticism (over-deliberation, standing still 'on the brink of beauty') leads to loss of spontaneity and helps produce insipid or maimed ideas; poets should not let critics dictate every turn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical, contrived structure and forced antitheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The most striking events occur in the shape of antitheses. The story is cut into the form of a parallelogram. There is the same systematic alternation of good and evil, of violence and repose ... as if nature were a machine constructed on a principle of complete contrast, to produce a theatrical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fables and narratives should arise naturally from the subject; do not contrive returns, disappearances, or plot conveniences merely for theatrical surprise, as this sacrifices reader satisfaction to authorial convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain intensity, momentum and unity (avoid desultory variety)
rubrics_metrics.description: His facility of production lessens the effect of, and hangs as a dead weight upon, what he produces. He exhausts attention by being inexhaustible. His variety cloys; his rapidity dazzles and distracts the sight. He wants intensity, strength, and grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exuberance and facile variety without focused energy dilute poetic effect; poets should cultivate momentum and concentrated emotional power rather than endless, detached impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire and burlesque — valued when performed with first-rate wit
rubrics_metrics.description: He has wit at will, and of the first quality. His satirical and burlesque poetry is his best: it is first-rate. His Twopenny Post-Bag is a perfect 'nest of spicery'; where the Cayenne is not spared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sharpness of satirical voice and disciplined burlesque are legitimate and often superior veins of poetic excellence when combined with genuine wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not attempt epic or tragic forms without fortitude of mind and suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Fortitude of mind is the first requisite of a tragic or epic writer. ... He ought not to have written Lalla Rookh ... It is not, however, a failure, so much as an evasion and a consequent disappointment of public expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long, elevated forms demand sustained seriousness and strength of temperament; attempting them without the necessary qualities risks evasion, disappointment, or mismatch between form and author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid morbid, self-absorbed passion that excludes wider interests
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing less poetical than this sort of unaccommodating selfishness. There is nothing more repulsive than this sort of ideal absorption of all the interests of others ... It is like a cancer, eating into the heart of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passionate intensity is valuable, but when passion becomes purely inward and self-consuming it repels rather than moves readers; poets should balance inner torment with outward engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power can compensate for defects, but does not erase them
rubrics_metrics.description: But still there is power; and power rivets attention and forces admiration. 'He hath a demon:' and that is the next thing to being full of the God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet's raw power of conception and expression may compel attention despite moral or stylistic flaws; critics should note both the coercive force and the accompanying moral/esthetic costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose elements congenial to the mind and preserve unity of keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the contracted range of his imagination, he has great unity and truth of keeping. He chooses elements and agents congenial to his mind, the dark and glittering ocean, the frail bark hurrying before the storm ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet should select motifs and images that fit his temperament and sustain consistent imaginative truth; unity in subject-matter and tone strengthens impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize when subjects belong to history rather than poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Buonaparte's character ... is a subject for history, and not for poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some contemporary or factual subjects may be inappropriate for poetic treatment because their demands are historical or documentary rather than lyric or imaginative; poetical treatment requires suitability of subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, flowing transparent style and broad accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: He describes that which is most easily and generally understood with more vivacity and effect than any body else. His style is clear, flowing, and transparent: his sentiments ... are common to him with his readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accessible diction and clear storytelling are virtues that secure wide readership; not every poet must seek recondite profundity—communication and vivacity are valid aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picturesque/vivid external description is a distinct poetic strength
rubrics_metrics.description: He has great intuitive power of fancy, great vividness of pencil in placing external objects and events before the eye ... His imagery is Gothic and grotesque. Few descriptions have a more complete reality, a more striking appearance of life and motion ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vivid pictorial imagination that places visible objects before the reader is a legitimate and powerful mode of poetry (e.g., Scott), though it may trade off with internal moral or philosophical depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality: being one's own subject (internal poetry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Wordsworth is the most original poet now living. He is the reverse of Walter Scott in his defects and excellences. His poetry is not external, but internal; it does not depend upon tradition ... he furnishes it from his own mind, and is his own subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original inward vision and unique subjective material distinguish great modern poetry; producing pieces that come from the poet's own mind can yield singular pathos and beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive faculty: the ability to form a coherent whole
rubrics_metrics.description: He cannot form a whole. He is totally deficient in all the machinery of poetry. His Excursion, taken as a whole, notwithstanding the noble materials thrown away in it, is a proof of this. The line labours, the sentiment moves slow, but the poem stands stock-still.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond isolated beautiful fragments, poets need constructive skill to assemble sustained longer works with momentum and progression; failure to do so leaves larger poems stagnant despite fine parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detached lyrical pieces may surpass larger works lacking cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Of many of the Lyrical Ballads, it is not possible to speak in terms of too high praise ... They open a finer and deeper vein of thought and feeling ... I do not think, however, there is anything in the larger poem equal to many of the detached pieces in the Lyrical Ballads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and poets should value the concentrated perfection of short pieces; a larger ambitious work must earn its length by unifying and building on its best parts rather than merely compiling them.
